app.name: X (formerly Twitter)
app.summary: With an X OAuth 2.0 app, an agent can read and post on X for each user who connects: posts, timelines, likes, follows, bookmarks, lists and DMs. Every API call is billed to the developer's prepaid credits.

verdict.headline: X has no app review, but there is no free tier: you prepay credits and pay for every user's API calls.

rationale.text: You create an app in the Developer Console (console.x.com) and turn on OAuth 2.0 in User authentication settings yourself. None of the docs I read describe a review before other users can authorize it. The real gate is money. Since February 2026 the X API is pay-per-use only. You buy credits up front and they are used up per request, for example $0.005 per post read and $0.015 per post created. The cost of every connected user's calls comes out of your balance, and requests are blocked when the balance reaches zero.

effort.firstConnection: About 30 minutes after signing in to console.x.com and buying credits

basis.text: X's docs describe app creation and OAuth setup as self-serve, with credits bought in the console. I found no published review or approval step for apps on pay-per-use. The time estimates are my inference from the number of console steps.

stages.name: Create the app and test with your own X account

limit.text: API calls need a credit balance. Reads of your own data (your posts, bookmarks, followers and so on) are billed at a lower 'Owned Reads' rate of $0.001 per resource, but only when the authenticated user is the app owner.

stages.name: Any X user can connect (pay-per-use)
stages.whoCanConnect: Any X account holder who authorizes the app

limit.text: All calls are billed to your credits at standard rates, capped at 3 million Post reads per monthly billing cycle. Requests are blocked when the balance hits zero or a spending limit you set is reached.

stages.name: Enterprise
stages.whoCanConnect: Any X user, at high volume

limit.text: Above 3M Post reads a month, or for custom rate limits, you need an Enterprise plan, which starts with X's enterprise interest form. Third-party reports put Enterprise contracts in the tens of thousands of dollars per month.

steps.title: Sign in to the Developer Console and accept the developer terms
steps.detail: Go to console.x.com and sign in with the X account that will own the app. Use a company-controlled account, not a personal one. Accept the developer agreement and policy when prompted.
steps.doneWhen: The Developer Console dashboard loads and shows a Create App option.

steps.title: Buy credits and set a spending limit
steps.detail: In the Developer Console, save a payment card and buy credits. Optionally turn on Auto-recharge (Recharge amount plus Trigger threshold) and set a Spending limit per billing cycle. Per X's docs, your first purchase earns $20 in free credits.
steps.doneWhen: The console shows a positive credit balance.

steps.title: Create App
steps.detail: Click Create App and enter a name, description and use case. Then generate credentials. Keys are shown only once.
steps.doneWhen: The app appears in the console with its keys generated.

steps.title: Configure User authentication settings for OAuth 2.0
steps.detail: In App settings > User authentication settings > Edit, enable OAuth 2.0 and pick Type of App = Web App (confidential client, which gets a Client Secret). Set App permissions (Read / Read and write / Read, write and DMs), fill in the consent-screen info (website, terms and privacy URLs), and add your exact callback URL. Matching is exact, including trailing slashes. Use https, with at most 10 callback URLs per app.
steps.doneWhen: The OAuth 2.0 Client ID and Client Secret are shown.

steps.title: Test authorization with your own account
steps.detail: Run the Authorization Code with PKCE flow (authorize at https://x.com/i/oauth2/authorize, token at https://api.x.com/2/oauth2/token). Request offline.access along with scopes such as tweet.read and users.read so you get a refresh token.
steps.doneWhen: A call to GET /2/users/me with the user token succeeds.

requirements.text: An X account to own the developer app, plus acceptance of X's developer terms.
A payment card and prepaid credits. X has offered no free tier since the February 2026 move to pay-per-use. Legacy Basic/Pro subscribers can opt in to pay-per-use from the console.
An exact-match https callback URL registered on the app.

The authorize endpoint (x.com/i/oauth2/authorize) resolves and shows an X login page to anonymous visitors. The page is rendered by JavaScript, so the probe could not see how X handles an invalid client_id.

nuances.text: Access tokens from the OAuth 2.0 PKCE flow are valid for only two hours. You get a refresh token only if you request the offline.access scope.
Billing is per resource returned and is deduplicated within a 24-hour UTC window. Fetching the same post again on the same UTC day is not charged twice, though X calls this a soft guarantee.
Creating a post that contains a URL costs $0.20 per request, against $0.015 for a plain post. This matters for agents that share links.
Auto-recharge fires at most once every 5 minutes and pauses at a zero or negative balance. A bursty agent can still hit 'out of credits' errors.
The cheap Owned Reads rate applies only when the authenticated user owns the developer app. Your connected customers' reads are billed at standard rates.
Changing app permissions means users must re-authorize before their tokens carry the new scope.
For local development, X requires http://127.0.0.1 rather than localhost in callback URLs.

blockers.title: Credit balance exhausted or spending limit reached
blockers.signal: API requests are blocked and return out-of-credits errors. A slightly negative balance blocks all requests until you top up.
blockers.nextMove: Add credits, raise the Spending limit, or set the auto-recharge amount high enough to cover 5 minutes of peak usage.

blockers.title: Monthly Post read cap
blockers.signal: Post reads stop after 3 million in a billing cycle on pay-per-use.
blockers.nextMove: Request Enterprise access through X's enterprise interest form.

blockers.title: Callback URL mismatch
blockers.signal: The authorize step fails, usually with a 'Something went wrong / You weren't able to give access to the App' page, when redirect_uri does not exactly match an allowlisted URL.
blockers.nextMove: Register the exact callback URL, trailing slash included, under User authentication settings.

agentCan: Draft the app name, description and use case for Create App
Fill in User authentication settings: app type, permissions, callback URLs, website, terms and privacy URLs
Draft privacy policy and terms pages for the consent screen
Run a test PKCE authorization and refresh-token exchange
Estimate monthly credit spend from planned endpoints using X's per-resource prices
youMust: Sign in with the X account that will own the app, and accept X's developer terms (a legal agreement)
Add a payment card, buy credits, and choose auto-recharge and spending limits (billing)
Complete the user consent step yourself during the first test authorization
Sign an Enterprise contract if you need more than 3M Post reads a month

uncertainties.question: Does X ever review or restrict pay-per-use apps before or after launch, for example over use-case policy or automation rules?
uncertainties.howToResolve: Read the current Developer Agreement and Policy at docs.x.com and ask on devcommunity.x.com.

uncertainties.question: What exact HTTP status and error body does the API return when credits run out?
uncertainties.howToResolve: Run a test call against a zero-balance account, or check the X API error reference.

uncertainties.question: Do per-endpoint rate limits (per user and per app per 15 minutes) still apply on top of pay-per-use billing, and at what values?
uncertainties.howToResolve: Check the rate limits page on docs.x.com and the response headers on real calls.

uncertainties.question: Third-party sources disagree on whether the pay-per-use read cap is 2M or 3M a month.
uncertainties.howToResolve: X's own pricing page currently says 3M. Confirm the live figure in the Developer Console.

providerContact.channel: X Developer Community forum (devcommunity.x.com) or support from the Developer Console
providerContact.draftMessage: Hi, we're building an AI agent where our users connect their own X accounts through OAuth 2.0 (Web App, confidential client) on a pay-per-use developer account. Is there any review or approval before third-party users can authorize our app? Which per-user and per-app rate limits apply on pay-per-use? And what error do API calls return when our credit balance runs out?
